1a

  • N: elī-ma | ana ṣūrim | ša šadî
  • T: ‘Go up on to the mountain crag,
  • L: elī-ma ← elû III “to go up, arise”; ana ← ana I “(aš-š... etc.) to, for (freq. abbr. an, with assimilation of n…”; ṣūrim ← ṣēru I “back, upperside”; ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; šadî ← šadû I “st. constr. šad(i)”
  • Note: See [RN117: 250]: “This line is — at least in part — an imperative counterpart of a narrative couplet in OB Schøyen₂ 27–8: īlīma Gilgāmeš ana ṣēr šadîm / ittanaplas kalīšunu ḫursānī. The meaning of ṣu₂-ri-im is taken from Semitic cognates, as proposed by [LS304: 217], but the new parallel offers another solution, that ṣu₂-ri-im is a spelling mistake for ṣe-ri-im. The traces after naplis were read a#-na# [eq]-li-im by [RN2652: 100], but neither copy supports this. Nor does any spelling of ḫursānī look possible at the end of the line.”
  • Parallels: cf. L I.4 OB "Schøyen₂" 27
ŠadOB1 o 1a. e#-li#-i-ma a-na ṣu₂-ri-im ša# KUR

2

  • N: šittam | ša ilī || anāku | ekmēku

  • L: šittam ← šittu I “sleep Bab. good, bad”; ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; ilī ← ilu I “pl. ilū, ilānu god, deity a or the god, also du.”; anāku ← anāku I “I”; ekmēku ← ekēmu I “to take away, deprive”

3a

  • N: ibrī | šuttam | aṭṭul
  • T: My friend, I saw a dream:
  • L: ibrī ← ibru I “friend, colleague”; šuttam ← šuttu I “pl. šunātu(m) dream š. naṭālu, amāru etc. to have a dream, to…”; aṭṭul ← naṭālu I “to look”
ŠadOB1 o 3a. ib#-ri šu-tam a-ṭu₂-ul

3b

  • N: kī laptat | kī nemiat | kī dalhat
  • T: how ominous it was, how desolate, how confused!
  • L: kī ← kī I “like”; laptat ← lapātu I “to touch, take hold of”; kī ← kī I “like”; nemiat ← nemû I “~ to be strange, disturbing? OB(lit.)”; kī ← kī I “like”; dalhat ← dalāhu I “to disturb, stir up Bab., OA, NA”
  • Note: See [RN117: 250]: “The emendation of the second verb follows von Soden. The word ne-ma-at defies obvious interpretation as it stands. Alongside the etymology put forward by von Soden (apû, ‘to become dim’), one thinks also of nawiʾat, ‘it was a desolation’ (on naw/mûm see the commentary on nu-ma-at in OB III 108).”
ŠadOB1 o 3b. ki la-<ap?>-ta#-at# ki ne-ma-at# ki# da#-al#-ha-at

4

  • N: anāku | rīmī (|) ṣērim | aṣṣabtānim
  • T: I had taken hold of (some) bulls from the wild —
  • L: anāku ← anāku I “I”; rīmī ← rīmu I “wild bull hunted”; ṣērim ← ṣēru I “back, upperside”; aṣṣabtānim ← ṣabātu I “to seize, take”
  • Note: See [RN117: 250]: “The remarkable plural ventive ending on the singular aṣṣabtānim elicited from von Soden another OB example, ki ta-da-am-mi-qu₂-nim in the poem often called ‘Man and his God’ ([nougayrol1952version: 246], re-edited by [RN1657: 192, 57], who translates ‘that you are well favoured’). Von Soden’s hope that a larger number of examples would eventually elucidate the usage has not yet been fulfilled. T. Jacobsen put forward an ingenious explanation in his discussion of the ‘ablative accusative’, analysing -nim instead as ‘departive’ -n- and ‘the expected, but hitherto missing, first singular common dative pronominal suffix -im, “for me”’ ([jacobsen1963akkadian: 26]). It remains a virtuoso position, unsubstantiated by further enquiry, though B. R. Foster also views the ending as expressing the first-person reflexive ([RN163: 41, fn. 42]: ‘I captured for myself’). Tournay and Shaffer’s emendation to first-person pl. niṣṣabtānim ([RN580: 109, fn. 11]) does not make parsing the suffix any easier. In our present state of knowledge these are desperate remedies and it seems wise to resort to neither of them. Thus I ignore the ending and keep to von Soden’s ‘ich packte gerade’.”
ŠadOB1 o 4. a-na#-ku AM-MEŠ# ṣe₂#-ri-im aṣ-ṣa-ab-ta-nim

5a

  • N: iš-šasêšu | qaqqaram | ilette
  • T: (one) was cleaving the ground with its bellowing,
  • L: iš-šasêšu ← ina I, šasû I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; qaqqaram ← qaqqaru I “pl. m. & f. ground, earth”; ilette ← letû I “split, divided jB lex. of wood, reed”
  • Note: See [RN117: 250]: “Though elsewhere in this tablet the scribe writes ina and ana in full — at least, as transliterated here — the spelling i-ša-se-šu very probably represents a pronunciation iš-šasêšu.”
ŠadOB1 o 5a. i-ša-se-šu qa-qa-ra-am i-le-te

5b

  • N: tarbuʾtašu | ittakkip | šamê
  • T: the cloud of dust it made was thrusting into the sky —
  • L: tarbuʾtašu ← tarbu'u I “dust (storm) Bab.”; ittakkip ← nakāpu I “to push, thrust Bab., NA”; šamê ← šamû I “mostly pl. tant. sky, heaven”
  • Note: See [RN117: 250]: “Lambert’s copy disposes of the problematical i-na tu-ur šamê (von Soden; van Dijk read i-x-x-ip?). I assume the verb is nakāpum I/2 separative, in the present tense to match ilette. Alternatively one might read itakkip < takāpum, ‘tinging the sky with colour’ (W. G. Lambert, personal communication).”

  • T: ‘My friend, the [god] to whom we are going,
  • L: [il]um ← ilu I “pl. ilū, ilānu god, deity a or the god, also du.”; ibrī ← ibru I “friend, colleague”; ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; nellakūšum ← alāku I “to go”

11

  • N: ul | rīmum-ma || nukkur | mimma
  • T: is he not the wild bull? He is something strange!
  • L: ul ← ul I “not Bab., to negate main clause”; rīmum-ma ← rīmu I “wild bull hunted”; nukkur ← nakāru I “to be(come) different”; mimma ← mimma I “and sim. anything, something”
  • Note: [RN117: 251]: “That the first clause is a question is made clear by the new parallel, OB Schøyen₂ 15: ul šadûm-mā nukkur mimma. In the matter of the last word I follow van Dijk, Sumer 14, p. 115, who in TIM IX, p. xi, vigorously rejects the reading mi-im-m[u-šu] proposed by [LS304: 216]. The latter restoration is ruled out for the following reasons: (a) the break appears to be too small to accept both mu and šu; (b) in order to align the ends of lines with the right-hand edge the scribe of this tablet routinely leaves a big gap before the last sign, but never before the last but one: thus only one sign is expected after mi-im; and (c) the parallels have mimma, OB Schøyen₂ 15 // 17 and MB Boǧ₂ obv. 23': ul ḫursān / mimma nuk[kur], the latter already noted by [RN2652: 116]. Landsberger’s translation of the present line, ‘nicht im mindesten ist der Wildstier widrig’, assumes an unusual word order in which the subject (rīmumma) splits the predicate (ul nukkur). Like von Soden I divide the present line into two clauses, with a caesura at their common boundary: úl | rīmúmma || núkkur | mímma.”
  • Parallels: cf. L I.4 OB "Schøyen₂" 15; cf. L I.4 OB "Boǧ₂" 21'c-22'a; cf. L I.4 OB "Boǧ₂" 23'a
ŠadOB1 r 2. u₂-ul ri-mu-um-ma# nu-ku-ur mi-im-ma#

12

  • N: zīmū | ša tāmuru || šamaš | namrum
  • T: The countenance that you saw was shining Šamaš,
  • L: zīmū ← zīmu I “face, appearance Bab., NA mostly pl.”; ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; tāmuru ← amāru I “to see”; šamaš ← Šamaš I; namrum ← nawru I “bright, shining of celestial bodies, as divine epith.”
  • Note: [RN117: 251]: “Van Dijk and von Soden suggested a reading of the first word as ri#-mu. The traces recorded on Lambert’s copy do not concur and I have adopted the reading proposed by J. Renger ([RN168CaRe: 96]). Now that the pattern of the dreams is more clearly understood, Renger’s objection to ri-mu, that in this tablet rīmum should be written with mimation, is reinforced by the consideration that the wild bull certainly symbolizes Ḫuwawa not Šamaš. Šamaš was well known for his zīmu, which was proverbially bright; the word became a technical term for the light emitted by the sun and other celestial bodies (see CAD Z, p. 121, and note Renger’s translation ‘Lichtgestalt’). This and the following line find a parallel in a couplet of Enkidu’s explanation of the avalanche dream (OB Schøyen₂ 21–2): u ša tāmuru Šamaš šarru / ina ūmi ša dannatim iṣabbat qātka.”
  • Parallels: cf. L I.4 OB "Nippur" a+6'; cf. L I.4 OB "Schøyen₂" 21; cf. L I.4 OB "Schøyen₃" b+7'; cf. L I.4 MB "Boğ₂" 26'
ŠadOB1 r 3. zi#-mu# ša ta-mu-ru {d}UTU na-am-ru-um#

17b

  • N: šipram | ša lā ibaššû | in[a] <mā>tim
  • T: a feat that does not (yet) exist in the land!’
  • L: šipram ← šipru I “pl. šiprū, Mari also šiprānu”; ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; lā ← lā I “not, no”; ibaššû ← bašû I “to be (at hand, available)”; in[a] ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; <mā>tim ← mātu I “f. land, country”
  • Note: [RN117: 251]: “On the penultimate sign see van Dijk, TIM IX, p. xi: ‘MA or MU impossible, hardly NA, most likely BE or NU, but NA is not excluded’. The emendations given here are confirmed by the appearance of the same line in the Yale tablet (OB III 17): šipram ša lā ibaššû ina mātim; cf. already [RN2652: 116, fn. 68]. The lack of plene marking of the final -û in this tablet may alternatively be explained as signifying a running together of ibaššû and ina (Lambert). Note the comparable spelling iṭ-hu-a-na (OB Schøyen₂ 26) for iṭḫû ana.”
  • Parallels: L I.4 OB "III" 17
ŠadOB1 r 7b. ši-ip-r[a]-am ša la i-ba-aš-šu-<u₂> i-n[a] <ma>-tim
